nasa-tm-19660026439-solar-evolution-with:
D. Ezer and A. G. W. Cameron, at the Institute for Space Studies in New York, ask a bold question in this paper. What if gravity itself has slowly changed over time? They test that idea, called varying-G cosmology, by recalculating how the Sun evolved under it.

Their model sequence extends their earlier work on early solar evolution. In the varying-G Sun, they find, lithium is used up less than in a constant-G Sun. The time to burn out the central hydrogen also shrinks, helped by much greater helium production. Their present-day model predicts a far higher neutrino output, a claim they note can be checked by experiment.
nasa-tm-19670009029-calculation-of-densi:
V. A. J. van Lint, Felix E. Geiger Jr., and D. K. Nichols describe a calculation method in this paper. Gamma rays passing through a material knock electrons loose, and those electrons damage the material's crystal structure. The authors show how to calculate the density of such defects to be expected.

Their method uses measured rates at which defects appear. It also uses the range-energy curve for electrons and the theoretical spectrum of Compton electrons. They work a specific case: silicon exposed to cobalt-60 gamma rays. Their result agrees reasonably with experimental data, and it corrects an earlier theoretical calculation.
nasa-tm-19680001779-compression-of-the-p:
H. A. Taylor Jr., H. C. Brinton, and M. W. Pharo III, at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this paper in November 1967. It studies the compression of the plasmasphere during geomagnetically disturbed periods. The plasmasphere is the fat torus of cold plasma co-rotating around Earth, and magnetic storms squeeze it inward.

Positive ion mass spectrometers aboard the OGO I and OGO III satellites measured hydrogen and helium ions directly during 1965 and 1966. Inside the plasmasphere, ion concentration fell gradually with height, but at the outer boundary, the plasmapause, it dropped abruptly. Sometimes it fell tenfold within a few hundred kilometers. That boundary moved inward and outward in step with planetary magnetic activity, showing large-scale expansion and contraction. During one stormy stretch in July 1966, the boundary was caught unusually low over the nightside Earth.
nasa-tm-19710015486-cosmic-antimatter-an:
F. W. Stecker, D. L. Morgan, and J. Bredekamp of the Goddard Space Flight Center issued this preprint in April 1971, numbered X-641-71-150. It asks whether antimatter exists on a large scale in the universe. When matter meets antimatter, both are destroyed and gamma rays result, so a cosmic gamma-ray glow could betray hidden antimatter.

The authors present early results from a detailed calculation of the gamma-ray spectrum that such annihilation would produce across the cosmos. Their calculated spectrum closely resembles the observed background above one million electron volts. They read that match as possible evidence for large-scale antimatter. The calculation folds in annihilation cross sections, absorption by the intergalactic medium, and photon scattering at high redshifts.
nasa-tm-19710025480-note-on-the-characte:
Kunitomo Sakurai wrote this note in July 1971, numbered X-693-71-267, on the sunspot groups that produce solar proton flares. Sakurai was a NASA associate with the University of Maryland. Most sunspot groups stay quiet, but a few erupt and spray high-energy protons into space, endangering astronauts and spacecraft.

The note argues that the production of solar cosmic rays grows as the gradient, the steepness, of a group's magnetic field increases. Such steep gradients form along with the rotating motion of sunspot groups. Groups whose polarity pattern is reversed prove especially effective at producing proton flares. Sakurai builds on Severny's work, which sorted proton flares into four classes tied to the magnetic field gradient.
